text: Mireya Elisa Moscoso Rodríguez, born on 1 July 1946 in Pedasí, Panama, is a Panamanian politician who served as the President of Panama from 1999 to 2004 and remains the country's first and only female president. Raised in a poor rural family as the youngest of six children, she lost her father when she was ten and began working as a secretary after high school. She joined the 1968 presidential campaign of Arnulfo Arias, a three-time president who was deposed by military coups, and married him after he went into exile in Miami, Florida, when she was 23 and he was 67. During this time, she studied interior design at Miami-Dade Community College. After Arias died in 1988, she took control of his coffee business and, on 29 September 1991, became president of the Arnulfista Party (PA), shortly after the U.S. invasion that ousted Manuel Noriega. In 1991, she married businessman Richard Gruber, adopting a son named Ricardo around 1992; they divorced in 1997. In the 1994 general election, she ran against PRD candidate Ernesto Pérez Balladares and salsa singer Rubén Blades, losing by 4% of the vote, with Pérez Balladares winning 33%, Moscoso receiving 29%, and Blades 17%. In the 1999 election, she defeated PRD candidate Martín Torrijos, who was chosen to represent the party after a failed constitutional referendum allowing Pérez Balladares to run again, by 7% (45% to 37%), running on a populist platform that included promises to support education, reduce poverty, and slow privatization. She took office on 1 September 1999, with her sister Ruby Moscoso de Young serving as First Lady due to her divorce. Facing a PRD-controlled Legislative Assembly and spending restrictions imposed by Pérez Balladares, she struggled to pass legislation and faced corruption scandals, including an unexplained gift of $146,000 in watches to legislators. Her approval rating dropped to 23% by 2001, and in 2003, the U.S. ambassador criticized her for growing corruption. By the end of her term, her presidency was widely seen as corrupt, incompetent, and weak. In 2004, she faced criticism for spending public funds on luxury clothing and jewelry, and was succeeded by her former rival Martín Torrijos, barred by the Constitution from a second term. Before leaving office, she pardoned four men convicted of plotting to assassinate Fidel Castro, sparking diplomatic tensions with Cuba and Venezuela, and issued pardons to 87 journalists for defamation, all of which were later overturned by the Supreme Court as unconstitutional in July 2008. After leaving office, she remained active in opposition politics, criticizing appointments and advocating for democratic oversight, and served on the Council of Women World Leaders at the Woodrow Wilson International Center for Scholars.
